round: review round 6's blocking finding - the hold bookkeeping, designed by the planner and ruled by the architect

proof.criterion: The blocking finding: the unconditional restore of a failed hand-back can take a role from a live holder in another process. A hold restored under a session this process has left is adopted by the next pass, becomes that claim's `previousSessionID`, and the listener puts a claimant's named predecessor into `supersedable` before it tests liveness, so the pane takes the role from the process now running that session.
proof.surface: The plugin's suite against the fake listener, driving the reviewer's six steps end to end, with the assertion taken from the listener's own rule rather than from any fix: this pane must not hold a role the listener names a live session for.
proof.command: cd packages/pi-envoy && bun test extensions/envoy.test.ts -t 'a role another process holds under a session this process left stays with that live session when this pane wants the role'
proof.observed: The case was written against the reviewer's trace before the design existed, and it is the judge of the change: at the round-6 head fabca81c it failed with `Expected: "ses_lk" / Received: "ses_lk_b"` - the pane holding a role the listener named a live session for - on three consecutive runs, and at this head it passes untouched and byte-identical. Every line of the trace was verified in the workspace before anything was built: the adoption at the `wanted` branch sets `claimedRoleSessionID = hold.id`; `settleRole` takes `supersedes` from it; `packages/envoy/cmd/listener/api.go:818-825` appends a matching predecessor to `supersedable` before the liveness test, its comment reading `so may the claimant's own predecessor, live or not`; `packages/envoy/internal/store/kv.go:612-614` lets the write through for any id in that slice.
proof.negativeControl: The case is the control for the whole design: it is not written to the fix, it was red before it, and it was never edited. What it does *not* judge was measured too, because this pull request has been wrong before about what a test proves: with the `sessionOpen(hold.id)` gate removed from the adoption it still passes. The gate's own test is `a pass that adopts a hold and fails the hand-back of the same role under another session records that hold for the listener to reap`, which is the single failure that mutation produces.

proof.criterion: A hold is exactly two facts, its role topic and the session id it was registered under, and both ledgers key on both. `abandonedHolds` keyed by topic alone meant two failed hand-backs of one role under two session ids collided and one was silently dropped - and a dropped hold is invisible to `observeAbandonedHold`, so the pane records a refusal it can never clear and stops reclaiming a role it would have had.
proof.surface: The plugin's suite: two holds of one role abandoned under two sessions, driven to the point where the pane either reclaims the role after the listener reaps the hold or has recorded a refusal and stopped.
proof.command: cd packages/pi-envoy && bun test extensions/envoy.test.ts -t 'holds of one role abandoned under two sessions are each waited out, neither read as a newer holder'
proof.observed: Written first, against the unedited readers, and red: `Expected: "ses_tw_c" / Received: undefined` - the pane never claimed the role after the reap, because the dropped hold made `observeAbandonedHold` read the refusal as a competitor's. The map is now keyed `<topic>@<id>` carrying `{ topic, id, lastSeen? }`, with its three readers following: `registerSession`'s reclaim deletes by key, `observeAbandonedHold` reads `<topic>@<holder>`, and `setEnvoyRole`'s single `delete(topic)` becomes the same topic sweep as the `pendingHandBacks` loop beside it. Green on three runs after the edit.
proof.negativeControl: The case failing against the unedited readers is itself the control, and it was run in that order deliberately rather than written after the fix. The whole file is the second control for a missed reader: 854 pass / 0 fail, where a reader left keying by topic alone shows up as another case going red rather than as this one passing.

proof.criterion: A failed hand-back is always abandoned, never classified against a captured host; and a hold becomes the role this process holds only while this process registers that session, read at the adoption. The second defect under the blocking one was that the restore loop classified with the host captured when its pass began, so a hold of a session the process had left was filed as pending - the one ledger the next pass adopts from - which is the opposite of what the function's own comment prescribes.
proof.surface: The plugin's suite, plus the function's signature: the capture must be unrepresentable rather than guarded.
proof.command: cd packages/pi-envoy && bun test extensions/envoy.test.ts ; grep -n 'settleEndedHolds' packages/pi-envoy/extensions/envoy.ts
proof.observed: The failed loop is one line - every failed hold written to `abandonedHolds` under its own key - so `host` is unused and the parameter is gone: `settleEndedHolds(wanted, live)`, with its one caller updated. The adoption gains `&& sessionOpen(hold.id)`, so that loop writes `claimedRoleTopic` and `holdUnconfirmed` and reads neither, which is the structural shape of round 5's defect and cannot return here. Nothing is lost by abandoning: `registerSession` moves every abandoned hold of the session it registers back into `pendingHandBacks` at each accepted registration, so a hold under a session this process still runs is pending again within one heartbeat interval. Three new cases pin it - the hand-back that fails under the session this process registers and is taken back by its next registration, and two variants of the one that fails under a session it has left and is waited out with no refusal recorded. Suite 854 pass / 0 fail.
proof.negativeControl: Mutating the failed loop to drop its failures turns twelve cases red, including the three new ones and the salvaged round-6 case, so no case here passes by the loop doing nothing. Mutating the adoption to drop the `sessionOpen(hold.id)` gate turns exactly one red, `a pass that adopts a hold and fails the hand-back of the same role under another session records that hold for the listener to reap`. Mutating it to never adopt turns four red. `envoy.ts` was restored byte-for-byte after each and verified by sha256 against `9fd2cd7888b1f8320b393ca745a3275ad31b981a6b8f92e5635874bbbeffa0b5`.

proof.criterion: The planner's fourth edit - delete `settleRole`'s branch that takes `supersedes` from `claimedRoleSessionID` - was to be built as designed. It cannot be: it breaks behaviour the suite already pins, and the decision belongs to the architect rather than to a condition invented in the round.
proof.surface: The whole plugin suite, with edits 1-3 committed and edit 4 applied exactly as written, then with edit 4 alone removed.
proof.observed: 76 failures with edit 4 applied; 853 pass / 0 fail with edit 4 alone removed, so the 75 extra are its own. 72 of them are the `every host switch against every establishment stage` matrix. The deleted branch has a second job nobody had named: it carries this process's own hold into a session it resumes whose records name that role, where `continuedBy` is a lineage of one, the kept branch never runs, the claim names no predecessor and the listener refuses it while the old session is still live - a resume losing its role for up to the session TTL. Representative failure: `a resume recording the role held settled when nothing else happens`, expected `ses_c_a`, received `ses_c`. Reported to the architect and the planner with the numbers and nothing built around it; the architect dropped edit 4 on the measurement, and the planner concurred and recorded it.
proof.negativeControl: The before-and-after over one edit is the control: the same suite, the same tree, edit 4 the only variable. A second measurement rules out the obvious narrowing: restricting the memory branch to a confirmed hold (`!holdUnconfirmed && ...`) leaves exactly one failure, an adopted hold whose pass hit an outage and was never confirmed but is still carried by a resume - so `holdUnconfirmed` does not separate the dangerous write from the needed one. Both experiments were reverted and the file re-hashed.

filesChanged: packages/pi-envoy/extensions/envoy.ts - `abandonedHolds` keyed `<topic>@<id>` with `{ topic, id, lastSeen? }` and its three readers; `settleEndedHolds(wanted, live)` with the host parameter gone, its failed loop one line of abandonment and its adoption gated by `sessionOpen(hold.id)`; its doc comment rewritten to the invariants; a comment at `observeAbandonedHold`'s `lastSeen` write stating the bound on misreading another process's refusal.
packages/pi-envoy/extensions/envoy.test.ts - the judge case for the reviewer's six-step trace, four cases for the new invariants, and one existing case whose route the ledger change moved.
trickyParts: The judge case was written before the design and never adjusted, which is the only reason it can judge the design. It was also measured for what it does not prove: the `sessionOpen(hold.id)` gate can be removed with the judge still green, and a different case catches that.

`settleEndedHolds`' own doc comment already stated the rule the code broke - a hold under a session the process has left belongs in `abandonedHolds` - and the captured host defeated it. The comment was rewritten with the edits rather than left to be rediscovered, since a comment asserting what the code does not do is how the last three rounds' defects entered.

The salvaged round-6 case now reaches its two hand-backs in the other order, because the first failure is abandoned and returns to `pendingHandBacks` behind the second at the next accepted registration. Its subject and surface are unchanged and its assertion is order-insensitive over the same two holds; it is one of the twelve cases that go red when the failed loop is mutated to drop failures, so it did not become weaker.
deviations: The planner's edit 4 was built and dropped on measurement, by the architect's ruling, and the door it would have closed is recorded in Not proven / risk with the writer named precisely - `setEnvoyRole`'s session-moved branch at envoy.ts:1957-1966, inside `if (!sessionOpen(id))`, writes `claimedRoleSessionID` for a session that is by construction not open, and `settleRole` can later name it as `previousSessionID`, which the listener honours against a live holder. It is pre-existing (c88a3a19 carries the same branch and write) and this round narrows what reaches it. The planner's discriminator for it, with its cost and its one-refresh-interval residual, is in plan.md v4, and the entry points there.

The planner's seventh test was written, measured and removed rather than weakened: its own assertion belonged to the dropped edit, and with that gone every behaviour left in it is already pinned by two existing cases, each demonstrated by mutation rather than by reading. The planner's T4 was not written either: `an abandoned hold whose session another process heartbeats again is the newer holder` already pins exactly that, and a duplicate case is worse than none.
discoveredComplexity: Four conditions have now been tried on this one loop - restore always, skip on topic, revert, and delete the memory branch - and each was wrong in a different direction. What separates this round is that the three edits come from stated invariants and remove possibilities rather than adding guards: the capture is absent from the signature, and both ledgers key on the two facts that identify a hold. The remaining question is a discriminator between carrying a hold the process itself still runs and naming a session another process may have resumed, which is recorded as a design rather than left as a trap.
